title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 3
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing practice test in two 32-minute modules (54 original questions), with an explanation for every answer and your score by skill.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice version of the Digital SAT **Reading and Writing** section: two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (64 minutes in total). Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four answer choices, just like the real test, which you take in the Bluebook app. All passages and questions are original.

items: **Sit the test in one go**, in a quiet place, with your phone away. Allow about 75 minutes: two 32-minute modules and a short pause between them.
**Keep the timer on.** You have about 1 minute 11 seconds per question. If a question is taking too long, choose your best answer, mark it in your head, and move on.
**Answer every question.** There is no penalty for wrong answers on the SAT, so never leave a blank.
**Within a module you may go back and change answers. Once you finish Module 1, do not go back to it** — in the real test you cannot return to Module 1 after Module 2 starts.

**The questions usually follow the real order:** Craft and Structure (vocabulary, purpose, two texts), then Information and Ideas (main idea, evidence, data, inferences), then grammar and punctuation, then transitions and notes questions at the end.

**Your result is a practice percentage, not an official SAT score.** Official scores (200–800 for this section) are calculated by the College Board in a different way, so do not try to convert your percentage into a scaled score.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
items: حل الامتحان مرة واحدة من غير توقف، في مكان هادي، والموبايل بعيد عنك.
شغّل التايمر: كل موديول 32 دقيقة، يعني حوالي دقيقة وربع لكل سؤال. لو سؤال أخد وقت كتير، اختار أحسن إجابة وكمّل.
جاوب على كل الأسئلة، مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط.
جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع وتغيّر، لكن أول ما تخلّص Module 1 ما ترجعلوش تاني، زي الامتحان الحقيقي بالظبط.
النتيجة اللي هتظهر لك نسبة مئوية للتدريب، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 3
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes per module. In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest questions, and Module 2 adapts to how well you did in Module 1 (it becomes harder or easier). Here all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Answer every question — there is no penalty for guessing.

questions.p: When linguist Amara Okafor recorded speakers of a small West African language, she noticed that older speakers used a special set of polite verbs whenever they spoke to elders. Younger speakers, by contrast, used these verbs only ______, mostly at weddings and other formal ceremonies, which suggests that the system is slowly falling out of everyday use.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: constantly
sparingly
eagerly
accurately
questions.e: "By contrast" and "only ... mostly at formal ceremonies" show that younger speakers rarely use the verbs, so "sparingly" (B) fits. "Constantly" (A) is the reverse trap: it contradicts the idea that the system is falling out of use. "Eagerly" (C) and "accurately" (D) say nothing about how often the verbs are used.

questions.p: Ordinary glass is brittle: a tiny crack can race through it in an instant. Chemist Rafael Lindqvist and his team have developed a glass containing tiny rubbery particles. When a spreading crack reaches one of these particles, the particle absorbs the crack's energy and ______ its progress, making the glass far less likely to shatter.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: accelerates
records
imitates
halts
questions.e: The particle absorbs the energy and makes shattering less likely, so it must stop the crack: "halts" (D). "Accelerates" (A) is the reverse of what the text describes. "Records" (B) and "imitates" (C) do not explain why the glass becomes harder to break.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of a nineteenth-century novel.
Mrs. Harrowgate received her nephew's letter with an air of perfect composure, folded it twice, and laid it beside her teacup as though it were nothing more than a bill from the grocer. Only the whiteness of her knuckles, as she gripped the arm of her chair, betrayed how deeply its contents had ______ her.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: unsettled
amused
bored
flattered
questions.e: Her calm is a mask; white knuckles gripping a chair show hidden distress, so the letter "unsettled" (A) her. "Amused" (B) and "flattered" (D) are pleasant feelings that do not match a tense grip. "Bored" (C) fits her calm surface but not the strong feeling her hands betray.

questions.p: For decades, many coaches told sprinters to hold long stretches just before a race, believing that this improved speed. A review of dozens of studies by sports scientist Lena Marsh has ______ that belief: athletes who held static stretches for more than a minute right before sprinting tended to run slightly slower, not faster.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: confirmed
inspired
undermined
exaggerated
questions.e: The review found the opposite of what coaches believed, so it weakened the belief: "undermined" (C). "Confirmed" (A) is the reverse trap. "Inspired" (B) would mean the review created the belief, and "exaggerated" (D) would mean it made the belief seem stronger.

questions.p: Fig trees and the tiny wasps that pollinate them depend completely on each other. Each fig species is usually pollinated by its own species of wasp, which lays its eggs inside the fig's enclosed flowers. As the young wasps develop, they eat some of the developing seeds; the females then leave, carrying pollen to another fig. Without its wasp, a fig tree cannot produce seeds, and without the fig, the wasp has nowhere to raise its young.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It presents a common belief about fig trees and then shows why it is mistaken.
It states that two organisms rely on each other and then explains how this relationship works.
It compares two species of fig wasps and explains why one is more successful.
It describes a threat to fig trees and then proposes a way to protect them.
questions.e: The first sentence states the mutual dependence, and the rest explains the process, so B is right. A is wrong because no belief is corrected; C because only one kind of relationship is described, not a competition between wasp species; D because no threat or solution is mentioned.

questions.p: Great Zimbabwe, a stone city in southern Africa built mainly between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, was for years credited by European colonial writers to foreign builders. Excavations in the twentieth century, beginning with those led by archaeologist Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929, showed that the city had been built by local African people, ancestors of today's Shona. Today its massive curved walls, made of stone blocks fitted together without mortar, are recognized as a major achievement of African architecture.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To explain how a mistaken belief about the builders of a historical site was corrected
To describe the techniques used to build stone walls without mortar
To argue that archaeological methods of the 1920s were unreliable
To compare Great Zimbabwe with other stone cities in Africa
questions.e: The text moves from a false colonial claim to the evidence that disproved it and the site's present recognition, so A states its purpose. B is too narrow: mortar-free walls are one detail. C reverses the role of the 1929 excavation, which helped correct the error. D is off-topic: no other cities are mentioned.

questions.p:
Text 1
Sociologist Priya Raman compared streets in one city with light, medium and heavy car traffic. Residents of quiet streets reported about three times as many friends living on their own street as residents of busy streets did. Raman concludes that heavy traffic damages the social life of a neighborhood.

Text 2
Urban researcher Daniel Osei studied busy streets that had wide sidewalks, benches and small shops at street level. On these streets, residents reported as much contact with neighbors as people on quiet streets. Osei argues that what matters most is whether a street gives people comfortable places to stop and meet.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Osei (Text 2) most likely respond to Raman's conclusion (Text 1)?
c: By claiming that car traffic has no effect at all on how people use a street
By arguing that Raman overstated how many friends residents of quiet streets have
By agreeing that cities should close all busy streets to cars
By suggesting that the effect Raman observed may depend on other features of a street, such as places to sit and shop
questions.e: Osei found busy streets with benches and shops where social contact was as high as on quiet streets, so he would say traffic alone does not decide the outcome (D). A is too extreme: Osei never says traffic has no effect. B questions Raman's data, which Osei does not discuss. C is unsupported: Osei focuses on street design, not closing streets.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original poem written in the style of the nineteenth century.
The oak that shaded my grandfather's door
Has watched a hundred summers come and go;
It does not mourn the leaves it held before,
Nor dread the coming of the winter snow.
It keeps its quiet counsel, root and bough,
And asks no more of heaven than the now.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: The speaker fears that the coming winter will destroy the old oak.
The speaker regrets that the oak will soon have to be cut down.
The speaker admires the oak's calm acceptance of the passing of time.
The speaker describes how the speaker's grandfather planted the oak long ago.
questions.e: The oak neither mourns the past nor dreads the winter and "asks no more ... than the now": the poem praises its calm acceptance (C). A reverses the poem: it is the oak that does not dread winter, and the speaker shows no fear. B is unsupported, and D adds a detail the poem never gives (the oak shaded the door; we are not told who planted it).

questions.p: Washing hands with soap is one of the cheapest ways to prevent the spread of infection, but many people wash too briefly to remove germs effectively. In one school district, a team led by nurse Halima Bello placed small devices above school sinks that played a twenty-second tune whenever the tap was turned on. Over one term, the average time students spent washing their hands rose from about six seconds to seventeen, and absences caused by stomach illnesses fell by nearly a quarter.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: A simple device that encouraged students to wash their hands for longer was linked to fewer illness-related absences.
Students in the school district preferred washing their hands while listening to music.
Most infections that spread in schools are caused by students who do not use soap.
Washing hands for twenty seconds is the only reliable way to prevent stomach illnesses.
questions.e: The text describes the tune devices, the longer washing times and the drop in absences, so A sums it up. B is off-topic: students' preferences are never measured. C is unsupported: the text does not say what causes most school infections. D is too extreme ("the only reliable way").

questions.p: Linguist Tomas Ferreira argues that when two languages are in contact for a long time, the words they borrow from each other most often name new objects, foods or practices rather than replacing basic everyday words such as "water" or "mother."
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's argument?
c: In one language, the native words for "water," "mother" and "hand" were all replaced by borrowed words within a century.
In a language that borrowed heavily from a trading partner's language, more than 80 percent of the borrowed words referred to tools, foods and customs introduced through trade.
Speakers of two languages in contact reported that borrowed words were usually easy to pronounce.
Languages that are in contact for a long time often develop similar patterns of sounds.
questions.e: Ferreira claims borrowings mostly name new things; a finding that most borrowed words named newly introduced tools, foods and customs supports this directly (B). A is the strongest trap but it weakens the argument: basic words were replaced. C (pronunciation) and D (sound patterns) are off-topic: they are not about which kinds of words are borrowed.

questions.p: In an original story written in a nineteenth-century style, Eliza Thorne lives with her brother in an old house on the edge of a country town. Throughout the story, the narrator presents Eliza as a young woman whose curiosity often overcomes her caution.
questions.q: Which quotation from the story most effectively illustrates this claim?
c: "Eliza kept the household accounts with a precision her brother admired and could never hope to imitate."
"She was fond of long walks in the country, and fonder still of returning from them in good time for tea."
"Eliza disliked surprises of every kind and arranged each week of her life with the greatest care."
"Though she had twice been warned that the cellar door was never to be opened, Eliza found herself, lamp in hand, descending its steps before the clock had struck nine."
questions.e: In D, Eliza knows the door is forbidden (caution) yet goes down the steps anyway (curiosity wins). A shows carefulness with money, not curiosity. B shows a pleasant habit with no risk. C is the reverse: it shows caution winning, not curiosity.

questions.p:
Hours of sleep the night before a test run and average 40-meter sprint time
Hours of sleep | Average sprint time (seconds)
4 | 6.21
6 | 6.05
8 | 5.94
10 | 5.92

Sports scientist Kofi Mensah measured sprint times of university athletes after nights with different amounts of sleep. He concluded that extra sleep improved sprint performance up to a point, but that the benefit became very small beyond eight hours.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Mensah's conclusion?
c: Athletes who slept 10 hours had the fastest average sprint time, 5.92 seconds.
Average sprint time after 6 hours of sleep was 6.05 seconds, faster than after 4 hours.
Average sprint time fell by 0.27 seconds between 4 and 8 hours of sleep but by only 0.02 seconds between 8 and 10 hours.
Average sprint time rose steadily as sleep increased from 4 to 10 hours.
questions.e: The conclusion has two parts: improvement up to 8 hours, then very little. C shows both (6.21 − 5.94 = 0.27; 5.94 − 5.92 = 0.02). A and B are true but half-right: they show improvement without the leveling off. D misreads the table: times fell, which means athletes got faster.

questions.p:
Share of entries to a regional photography competition, by format
Year | Shot on film (%) | Shot digitally (%)
2015 | 9 | 91
2020 | 14 | 86
2025 | 21 | 79

When digital cameras became cheap and powerful, many observers predicted that film photography would soon disappear. Records from one regional photography competition suggest otherwise: the share of entries shot on film ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
c: rose from 9 percent in 2015 to 21 percent in 2025.
was lower than the share shot digitally in every year shown.
fell from 91 percent in 2015 to 79 percent in 2025.
stayed at 14 percent between 2020 and 2025.
questions.e: To challenge the prediction that film would disappear, the text needs film's share growing: 9% to 21% (A). B is true but does not contradict the prediction. C uses the digital column, not the film column. D misreads the table: the film share rose from 14% to 21%.

questions.p: Fireflies use patterns of flashing light to find mates, and each species has its own pattern. Entomologist Ines Duarte compared fields beside newly lit roads with dark fields a short distance away. A year after the lights were installed, she found far fewer firefly larvae in the lit fields, even though the plants and soil in both kinds of field were very similar. Because the main difference between the fields was the amount of artificial light, Duarte suggested that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: fireflies near roads produce brighter flashes than fireflies in dark fields do.
the soil near roads contains chemicals that are harmful to firefly larvae.
artificial light may make it harder for adult fireflies to see one another's signals and find mates.
firefly larvae prefer to live in fields with taller plants.
questions.e: Light was the main difference, and fireflies find mates by seeing flashes; if lights hide the signals, fewer adults mate and fewer larvae appear the next year (C). A is unsupported. B and D contradict the text, which says soil and plants were very similar.

questions.p: Stainless steel resists rust because of the chromium it contains. When the metal is exposed to air, the chromium forms a thin, invisible layer of oxide on its ______ this layer blocks oxygen and water from reaching the iron underneath.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: surface,
surface;
surface
surface, which
questions.e: Both parts are independent clauses ("the chromium forms ..." / "this layer blocks ..."), so a semicolon joins them (B). A is a comma splice and C is a run-on. D makes "which this layer blocks" ungrammatical.

questions.p: The new engineering museum in Port Alder displays three early machines from the region's factories: a weaving loom, built in 1802; a steam pump, built in 1824______ and a printing press, built in 1851.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: SAT/ACT extra rule: when list items already contain commas, semicolons separate the items. The first item ends with a semicolon, so the second must too (D). A comma (A) mixes the two systems and blurs the items; a colon (B) cannot appear inside a list; no punctuation (C) runs two items together.

questions.p: Satyajit Ray's first feature film—Pather Panchali, released in 1955______ was made on such a small budget that filming stopped several times while Ray searched for more money.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The extra information begins with a dash, so it must close with a dash: dash ... dash (A). A comma (B) creates a mismatched pair. No punctuation (C) leaves the extra information open, and a semicolon (D) separates the subject "film" from its verb "was made."

questions.p: In his 1989 book on community life, sociologist Ray Oldenburg argued that cafés, barbershops and other informal gathering ______ as "third places": spaces that are neither home (the first place) nor work (the second), where neighbors meet as equals.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: spots, serve
spots—serve
spots serve
spots; serve
questions.e: "Cafés, barbershops and other informal gathering spots" is the subject and "serve" is its verb; no punctuation may come between them (C). A, B and D all wrongly split the subject from its verb, and the semicolon in D would also need an independent clause on each side.

questions.p: Japan's tea-drinking culture is often traced to a single ______ the Buddhist monk Eisai, who brought tea seeds back from China in 1191 and later wrote one of the first Japanese books about the drink.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: traveler;
traveler:
traveler, and
traveler, he was
questions.e: The first part is a complete sentence, and what follows names the traveler, so a colon introduces the explanation (B). A is wrong because a semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "the Buddhist monk Eisai, who ..." is not one. C adds "and" with no clause to join, and D creates a comma splice.

questions.p: The collection of insect specimens assembled by nineteenth-century naturalist Edmund Pike, which includes more than 4,000 beetles from the rainforests of Borneo, ______ now kept in a climate-controlled room at a university museum.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: are
were
have been
is
questions.e: The subject is "The collection" (singular); "of insect specimens" and the "which" clause are only modifiers. So the verb is singular "is" (D). A, B and C are plural verbs that agree with "specimens" or "beetles": the nearest-noun trap. "Were" is also the wrong tense for "now."

questions.p: Bamboo stalks are remarkably strong for their weight. Engineers who study them have found that ______ hollow, segmented structure helps the stalks bend without breaking in strong winds.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: their
its
it's
they're
questions.e: The pronoun refers to "Bamboo stalks" (plural), so the plural possessive "their" is needed (A). B is singular and would refer to "bamboo" or "weight," not the stalks. C means "it is" and D means "they are"; neither is possessive.

questions.p: Before 1900, most cameras were large, costly and difficult to use, so photography was mainly a hobby for professionals and the wealthy. Introduced by the Eastman Kodak Company in 1900 and sold for just one dollar, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: millions of ordinary people were able to take photographs for the first time with the Brownie camera.
the Brownie camera allowed millions of ordinary people to take photographs for the first time.
taking photographs became possible for millions of ordinary people with the Brownie camera.
the first time millions of ordinary people could take photographs came with the Brownie camera.
questions.e: The opening modifier describes something that was introduced and sold, so the camera must come right after the comma (B). A, C and D are dangling modifiers: they say that people, "taking photographs" or "the first time" were sold for one dollar.

questions.p: For centuries, smallpox killed millions of people around the world. In 1967, the World Health Organization began an intensified campaign to vaccinate people and to trace every new case of the disease. ______ in 1980 the organization declared that smallpox had been eradicated, making it the first human disease to be wiped out.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Similarly,
For example,
Eventually,
Nevertheless,
questions.e: The campaign started in 1967 and succeeded in 1980, so the second event comes later in time and results from a long effort: "Eventually" (C). A needs a similar second case; B needs an example of a general claim; D needs an obstacle that the result happened despite.

questions.p: Many city planners have assumed that building more roads will reduce traffic jams. Studies of urban traffic, ______ have repeatedly found that new roads tend to fill with additional drivers within a few years, leaving congestion close to where it started.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: therefore,
for instance,
in addition,
however,
questions.e: The studies' finding goes against the planners' assumption, so a contrast word is needed: "however" (D). A would mean the finding follows from the assumption. B would make the studies an example of the assumption, and C would add a point in the same direction.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Before the fifteenth century, Korean was written mainly with Chinese characters.
• Few ordinary Koreans had the time to learn thousands of these characters.
• King Sejong the Great created a new alphabet, Hangul, in 1443; it was announced to the public in 1446.
• Sejong wanted ordinary people, not only scholars, to be able to read and write.
• The shapes of Hangul's consonants are based on the positions of the mouth and tongue when the sounds are made.
questions.q: The student wants to explain why Hangul was created. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: King Sejong the Great created Hangul in 1443 so that ordinary Koreans, not only scholars, could learn to read and write.
The shapes of Hangul's consonants are based on the positions of the mouth and tongue.
Hangul was created in 1443 and announced to the public three years later, in 1446.
Hangul was created by King Sejong the Great, who ruled Korea in the fifteenth century.
questions.e: Only A gives the reason ("so that ordinary Koreans ... could learn to read and write"). B describes how the letters look, C gives dates, and D says who created it; none explains why.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A beam bridge is the simplest type of bridge: a flat deck rests on supports at each end or along its length.
• Beam bridges are best suited to short spans.
• In a suspension bridge, the deck hangs from cables that pass over tall towers.
• Suspension bridges can span very long distances.
• The main span of Japan's Akashi Kaikyō Bridge, a suspension bridge, is 1,991 meters long.
questions.q: The student wants to contrast the two types of bridges in terms of the distances they can cross. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The main span of the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge, a suspension bridge in Japan, is 1,991 meters long.
In a beam bridge, the deck rests on supports; in a suspension bridge, the deck hangs from cables.
A beam bridge, the simplest type of bridge, has a flat deck that rests on supports.
While beam bridges are best suited to short spans, suspension bridges can cross very long distances.
questions.e: D contrasts the two types on distance (short spans vs. very long distances). A gives a distance for only one bridge. B is the strongest trap: it contrasts the types, but by structure, not by distance. C describes only one type.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cai Lun was an official at the court of the Chinese emperor during the Han dynasty.
• In 105 CE, he presented the emperor with an improved method of making paper.
• His paper was made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets.
• The new paper was cheaper and lighter than bamboo strips or silk, the main writing materials of the time.
questions.q: The student wants to introduce Cai Lun and his achievement to an audience unfamiliar with him. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Cai Lun's paper was made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets.
Cai Lun, an official at the Chinese emperor's court, presented an improved method of making paper in 105 CE.
In 105 CE, Cai Lun presented his method to the emperor.
Paper made from tree bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets was cheaper than silk.
questions.e: An unfamiliar audience needs to know who Cai Lun was and what he did; B gives both. A assumes readers already know who he is. C does not say what "his method" was. D never mentions Cai Lun at all.

questions.p: Some critics describe the large number of English loanwords in modern Japanese as a sign of cultural surrender. Linguist Kenji Arai finds this view ______: in his analysis, Japanese speakers reshape borrowed words so thoroughly—shortening them, changing their meanings and combining them with native words—that the results are distinctly Japanese creations.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: persuasive
novel
simplistic
ambiguous
questions.e: Arai shows that borrowing is a complex creative process, so he thinks the critics' view ignores that complexity: "simplistic" (C). A is the reverse: he disagrees with the view. B says the view is new, which the text does not discuss. D means unclear, but his objection is that the view is wrong, not unclear.

questions.p: Polymer chemist Odile Fontaine has created a plastic that can be broken down into its original building blocks and rebuilt again and again without losing strength. Earlier recyclable plastics grew weaker every time they were melted and reshaped, so their usefulness was ______: after a few cycles, the material had to be thrown away.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: finite
obscure
immediate
redundant
questions.e: The earlier plastics could be reused only a few times before being thrown away, so their usefulness had a limit: "finite" (A). B means hard to understand or little known; C means happening at once; D means unnecessary. None describes a limited number of uses.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of a nineteenth-century novel.
The vicar was not, by temperament, a man given to ______. He weighed every word before he allowed it to leave his lips, and more than one parishioner had grown weary of waiting for the end of a sentence he had plainly begun with the greatest care.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: deliberation
melancholy
generosity
impetuosity
questions.e: The vicar weighs every word and speaks with great care, so he is not given to acting or speaking hastily: "impetuosity" (D). A is the reverse trap: he is full of deliberation, and the sentence says he is NOT given to the blank. B and C describe sadness and kindness, which the text never discusses.

questions.p: Although altitude training is widely used by distance runners, its benefits are far from ______. In a study led by physiologist Maren Holt, some runners improved their race times markedly after four weeks of training at high altitude, while others showed no change at all, and a few actually became slower.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: trivial
uniform
documented
temporary
questions.e: The study shows very different results for different runners, so the benefits are not the same for everyone: "far from uniform" (B). A would mean the benefits are large, but the text stresses variation, not size. C would mean the benefits are unrecorded, yet the study records them. D is off-topic: how long the effects last is not discussed.

questions.p: In many forests, older trees are linked to younger ones through underground networks of fungi that grow around their roots. Some writers have claimed that, through these networks, large "mother trees" deliberately send food to their own seedlings. __A team led by ecologist Rhea Castell, however, reviewed dozens of field studies and found that few of them showed resources moving between trees in ways that clearly helped seedlings survive.__ The team concluded that the networks are real but that popular claims about their role have run far ahead of the evidence.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It offers an example that supports the claim that mother trees feed their seedlings.
It explains how underground fungal networks form between the roots of trees.
It presents a finding that casts doubt on the claim described in the previous sentence.
It introduces a conclusion that the final sentence then rejects.
questions.e: "However" signals that the review challenges the "mother tree" claim just mentioned (C). A is the reverse: the review undermines the claim. B is off-topic: the sentence is about evidence, not how networks form. D is wrong because the final sentence builds on the review's finding rather than rejecting it.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original poem written in the style of the nineteenth century.
When first I came, the city seemed all stone,
A maze of smoke where no one knew my name;
I walked its crowded lanes as one alone.
But years have passed, and now each street I roam
Returns my greeting, door by lamplit door,
And what was foreign I must call my home.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: The speaker describes a city and then explains why the speaker has decided to leave it.
The speaker compares two cities in which the speaker has lived at different times.
The speaker identifies a problem in a city and then proposes a way to solve it.
The speaker recalls a first impression of a place and then describes how that impression has changed over time.
questions.e: Lines 1–3 give the speaker's lonely first impression; "But years have passed" turns to his present feeling that the city is home (D). A reverses the ending: he now calls the city home. B is wrong because only one city appears. C misreads the poem as a problem-and-solution text.

questions.p:
Text 1
Many film historians argue that the arrival of synchronized sound in the late 1920s harmed cinema as an art. Early sound cameras were so noisy that they had to be shut inside soundproof booths, so for several years cameras hardly moved, and films became stiff and stage-like.

Text 2
Film scholar Nadia Ferro accepts that the first sound films were often static. But she points out that within a few years, filmmakers had developed soundproof covers for cameras and microphones on long poles, freeing the camera again. Sound, she argues, then gave filmmakers dialogue, music and sound effects—storytelling tools that silent films had lacked.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Ferro (Text 2) most likely respond to the historians' argument in Text 1?
c: She would accept that sound first limited camera movement but argue that this problem was brief and was outweighed by the new possibilities sound created.
She would reject the historians' claim that early sound cameras were noisy and difficult to move.
She would argue that silent films had been just as static as the first sound films.
She would agree that the arrival of sound permanently reduced the artistic quality of cinema.
questions.e: Ferro accepts the early stiffness but says it was quickly solved and that sound added storytelling tools (A). B is wrong because she accepts the historians' description of early films. C is unsupported: she never compares sound films with silent films' movement. D reverses her view: she thinks the harm was temporary.

questions.p: Historians once pictured the Silk Road as a single highway along which merchants carried goods all the way from China to the Mediterranean. More recent research paints a different picture. Most traders, it now appears, traveled only short distances, exchanging goods with others at regional markets; very few individuals ever crossed the whole route. Many of the most important things that spread along it—religions, technologies and words—moved gradually from one community to the next rather than in single long journeys.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Religions and technologies spread along the Silk Road much faster than goods did.
Recent research suggests that the Silk Road was a network of connected local exchanges rather than one route traveled from end to end.
Few merchants traveled the full length of the Silk Road because the journey was too dangerous.
The goods carried along the Silk Road were less valuable than historians once believed.
questions.e: The text contrasts the old "single highway" view with new evidence of short, local exchanges (B). A invents a comparison of speed. C adds a reason (danger) the text never gives: a half-right trap. D is off-topic: the value of goods is not discussed.

questions.p: Researcher Tobias Lindgren hypothesizes that the advantage home teams have in professional soccer comes mainly from the pressure that crowds put on referees, rather than from players' familiarity with their own stadium.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindgren's hypothesis?
c: Home teams won more often in stadiums they had used for many years than in newly built stadiums.
Away teams that traveled long distances to matches lost more often than away teams that traveled short distances.
Referees who worked in stadiums with large crowds had more years of experience than referees in small stadiums.
In a season when matches were played without spectators, home teams still played in their own stadiums, but referees stopped favoring them and the home advantage largely disappeared.
questions.e: In D, the crowd is removed but the familiar stadium remains; because the referees stopped favoring home teams and the advantage vanished, the cause points to the crowd, not familiarity. A is the strongest trap but supports the rival explanation (familiarity). B concerns travel fatigue, and C concerns referees' experience; neither tests the crowd effect.

questions.p: In an original poem written in a nineteenth-century style, an old man looks back on the hard years his family spent on a farm in the hills. In the poem, the speaker suggests that memory makes past hardships seem gentler than they really were.
questions.q: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
c: "The winter that once cut us to the bone / Now glows, recalled, like embers on a hearth."
"We gathered wood each morning in the frost / And counted every stick against the cold."
"I hope the years ahead will bring us ease, / And kinder winters than the ones we knew."
"The hearth is cold, the house is empty now, / And no one tends the fire we used to keep."
questions.e: A shows a harsh winter ("cut us to the bone") that now "glows" warmly in memory: the hardship has been softened. B describes the hardship but not how memory changes it. C looks to the future, not to memory. D describes present loss rather than a softened past.

questions.p:
Pollinator visits per hour to crop flowers at different distances from a wildflower strip
Distance from strip (m) | Farm A | Farm B
10 | 42 | 38
50 | 31 | 30
100 | 18 | 27
200 | 9 | 25

Ecologist Sunita Varma studied whether wildflower strips planted along field edges increase pollinator visits to nearby crops. At both farms, visits declined with distance from the strip, but Varma noted that the decline was much steeper at Farm A. She suggested that the hedgerows found throughout Farm B, which give bees places to nest, may explain the difference.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Varma's observation?
c: At both farms, crops 10 meters from the strip received more visits than crops 50 meters away.
At 50 meters from the strip, Farm A and Farm B received almost the same number of visits per hour.
At Farm A, visits fell from 42 per hour at 10 meters to 9 per hour at 200 meters, while at Farm B they fell only from 38 to 25.
At 10 meters from the strip, Farm B received fewer visits per hour than Farm A did.
questions.e: Varma's observation compares how steeply visits fall at each farm, so the answer must show the full decline at both: 42→9 vs. 38→25 (C). A shows a decline at both farms but not which is steeper. B and D are true single-distance comparisons that say nothing about the rate of decline.

questions.p:
Protected bike lanes and walking or cycling to work in four cities
City | Lanes built 2015–2023 (km) | Residents walking or cycling to work, 2015 (%) | 2023 (%)
Ardent | 120 | 11 | 19
Belmore | 85 | 14 | 20
Calloway | 40 | 9 | 12
Dunmore | 15 | 13 | 14

Urban researcher Leila Haddad claims that, among these four cities, those that built more kilometers of protected bike lanes saw larger increases in the share of residents who walk or cycle to work.
questions.q: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Haddad's claim?
c: Belmore had the highest share of residents walking or cycling to work in 2015, at 14 percent.
Ardent, which built 120 kilometers of lanes, saw its share rise by 8 percentage points, while Dunmore, which built 15 kilometers, saw a rise of only 1 point.
Calloway had a lower share of residents walking or cycling to work than Ardent did in both 2015 and 2023.
Dunmore's share in 2023 was higher than Calloway's, even though Dunmore built fewer kilometers of lanes.
questions.e: The claim links kilometers built to the size of the increase; B compares the city that built the most (120 km, +8) with the one that built the least (15 km, +1). A gives a starting level, not an increase. C compares levels, not increases. D is the trap: it compares levels in 2023 and seems to go against the claim, but Dunmore's increase (+1) was actually smaller than Calloway's (+3).

questions.p: In many unrelated languages, the word for "mother" contains an m sound, as in Swahili mama and Mandarin mā. One common explanation is that m is among the first consonants babies produce, since it requires only closing and opening the lips. Linguist Rosa Imbert points out, however, that babies also produce b and p sounds very early, yet words for "mother" built on these sounds are far less common than words built on m. If Imbert is correct, then ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: babies learn to produce the m sound later than they learn the b and p sounds.
the words for "mother" in Swahili and Mandarin were borrowed from the same source language.
the ease of producing a sound early in life cannot by itself explain why m is so common in words for "mother."
words for "mother" in most languages originally began with b or p sounds.
questions.e: If b and p are just as easy and early as m but rarely appear in "mother" words, then early ease alone cannot explain the pattern (C). A contradicts the text, which says b and p are also produced very early. B and D are unsupported claims about history that the text never makes.

questions.p: In 1856, Henry Bessemer announced a process for making steel cheaply by blowing air through melted iron to burn away impurities. Bessemer's own steel was strong, but many ironmakers who bought the right to use his process produced brittle, useless metal. Investigators later found that Bessemer had happened to use iron that was naturally low in phosphorus, an impurity that the air-blowing process did not remove. This finding suggests that the other ironmakers' failures most likely resulted from ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: using iron that contained more phosphorus than the iron Bessemer had used.
using iron that contained less phosphorus than the iron Bessemer had used.
blowing air through the melted iron for too short a time.
Bessemer's refusal to share the details of his process with them.
questions.e: Bessemer succeeded because his iron was low in phosphorus, which the process could not remove; the others' brittle steel therefore most likely came from iron higher in phosphorus (A). B is the reverse trap. C is unsupported: the text says the process cannot remove phosphorus at all. D contradicts the text, which says the ironmakers bought the right to use the process.

questions.p: The kingdom of Aksum, centered in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, issued its own gold, silver and bronze coins from around the late third century ______ it was one of very few states of its time anywhere in the world to mint coins in gold.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: CE, indeed,
CE, indeed
CE indeed,
CE; indeed,
questions.e: Two independent clauses are joined, and "indeed" is a transition word, not a conjunction, so a semicolon must come before it and a comma after it (D). A and B are comma splices: a comma plus "indeed" cannot join two sentences. C is a run-on.

questions.p: Published in 1958, Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe's first ______ Things Fall Apart, has been translated into more than fifty languages and is read in schools around the world.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: novel
novel,
novel—
novel:
questions.e: Achebe had only one first novel, so its title is extra (non-essential) information and needs a pair of commas; the closing comma already follows the title (B). A leaves an unmatched closing comma between subject and verb. C mixes a dash with a comma. D is wrong because the words before the colon are not a complete sentence.

questions.p: Seeking a coating that could protect jet-engine parts from extreme heat, chemist Yuki Mori tested more than a dozen ceramic materials. The three that performed best in her trials ______ silica, alumina and zirconia.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: were
were:
were;
were—
questions.e: "The three ... were" is not a complete sentence until the list is added, so no punctuation should separate the verb from its complement (A). A colon (B) must follow a complete sentence. A semicolon (C) needs an independent clause on both sides. A dash (D) also wrongly breaks the verb from what completes it.

questions.p: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry back to their nests. Instead, they chew the leaves into a pulp and use it to grow a fungus in underground ______ fungus is the colony's main source of food.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: gardens, this
gardens this
gardens; this
gardens, which this
questions.e: "They ... use it to grow a fungus in underground gardens" and "this fungus is the colony's main source of food" are both independent clauses, so a semicolon is needed (C). A is a comma splice; B is a run-on. D is ungrammatical: "which" and "this fungus" cannot both begin the clause.

questions.p: Along the walls of the gallery's main room ______ a series of black-and-white portraits by Malick Sidibé, the Malian photographer celebrated for his images of young people in Bamako during the 1960s.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: hang
are hanging
have hung
hangs
questions.e: The sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. The subject is "a series" (singular), so the verb is "hangs" (D). A, B and C are plural, matching "walls" or "portraits" instead of the true subject: the nearest-noun trap.

questions.p: When the first paved road finally reached the mountain town of Valmora in 1931, the town's blacksmith, Anton Reyes, ______ horseshoes and cart wheels for nearly forty years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: has been making
had been making
is making
will have made
questions.e: His work began before 1931 and continued up to that past moment, so the past perfect progressive is needed: "had been making" (B). A links the action to the present, not to 1931. C is present tense, and D is future tense; both clash with a past event in 1931.

questions.p: Sociologists Ana Ruiz and Joon Park spent three summers measuring temperatures in different neighborhoods of the same city. The two ______ joint report found that streets lined with mature trees were, on average, several degrees cooler in the afternoon than streets without trees.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: researcher's
researchers
researchers'
researchers's
questions.e: The report belongs to two researchers, so the plural possessive is needed: "researchers'" (C). A is singular possessive (one researcher). B is a plain plural with no possession. D is not a correct form: a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

questions.p: In the 1860s, most portrait photographers aimed for perfect sharpness, believing that a photograph's value lay in its precise recording of detail. A few photographers, ______ deliberately left their portraits slightly out of focus, arguing that softness could reveal a sitter's character better than sharp detail could.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: however,
therefore,
similarly,
in other words,
questions.e: Most photographers wanted sharpness; a few did the opposite, so a contrast word is needed: "however" (A). B would make the blurred portraits a result of the belief in sharpness. C needs the same approach, not the opposite one. D would mean the second sentence restates the first.

questions.p: Gold is prized partly because it hardly tarnishes: unlike iron or copper, it barely reacts with oxygen or water. ______ gold jewelry that has been buried in the ground for thousands of years often looks nearly new when archaeologists uncover it.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Even so,
In contrast,
Before then,
As a result,
questions.e: Gold does not react with oxygen or water, and that is why buried gold still looks new; the second sentence is a result (D). A would mean the jewelry looks new despite gold's properties, the reverse of the logic. B needs two different things compared, but the same metal is discussed. C is a time word with no earlier event to refer to.

questions.p: The American mechanic Elisha Otis did not invent the elevator; platforms raised and lowered by ropes had been used for centuries. ______ what Otis introduced in the 1850s was a safety brake that stopped a platform from falling if its rope broke—an innovation that made passenger elevators in tall buildings practical.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Similarly,
Rather,
Consequently,
For instance,
questions.e: The text corrects a mistaken idea (Otis invented the elevator) and then states what he really did, which is the job of "Rather" (B). A needs a similar case. C is the strongest trap, but the brake is not a result of earlier platforms existing. D needs an example of the first sentence's point.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The emerald ash borer is a beetle native to northeastern Asia.
• It was first detected in North America in 2002, near Detroit, Michigan.
• Its larvae feed on the inner bark of ash trees.
• This feeding cuts off the flow of water and nutrients through the tree.
• The beetle has killed hundreds of millions of ash trees in North America.
questions.q: The student wants to explain why the emerald ash borer is so harmful to ash trees. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The emerald ash borer has killed hundreds of millions of ash trees in North America.
The emerald ash borer, a beetle native to northeastern Asia, was first detected in North America in 2002.
First found near Detroit, Michigan, the emerald ash borer is a beetle that feeds on ash trees.
The emerald ash borer's larvae feed on the inner bark of ash trees, cutting off the flow of water and nutrients that the trees need.
questions.e: "Why" requires the cause of the damage: the larvae cut off water and nutrients (D). A is the strongest trap: it shows HOW MUCH harm the beetle does, not why. B gives origin and date, and C says it feeds on ash trees without explaining why this kills them.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Esperanto is a constructed language created by L. L. Zamenhof and first published in 1887.
• Zamenhof hoped it would become an easy second language for international communication.
• Toki Pona is a constructed language created by Sonja Lang and first shared in 2001.
• Toki Pona has a vocabulary of only about 120 words.
• Lang designed it to encourage speakers to focus on simple, basic ideas.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Esperanto and Toki Pona. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Like Esperanto, which was published in 1887, Toki Pona, first shared in 2001, is a constructed language deliberately designed by one person.
Esperanto was meant for international communication, whereas Toki Pona was designed to encourage a focus on simple ideas.
Toki Pona, created by Sonja Lang, has a vocabulary of only about 120 words.
Esperanto was created by L. L. Zamenhof more than a century before Toki Pona was first shared.
questions.e: A uses "Like" and names what the two languages share: each is a constructed language designed by an individual. B is the strongest trap: it uses both languages but emphasizes a difference in purpose. C discusses only Toki Pona. D contrasts their dates.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A camera obscura is a dark room or box with a small hole in one wall.
• Light passing through the hole projects an upside-down image of the outside scene onto the opposite wall.
• The scholar Ibn al-Haytham described this effect in his Book of Optics in the early eleventh century.
• Some Renaissance painters used camera obscuras as drawing aids.
• The photographic camera works on the same basic principle.
questions.q: The student wants to explain the camera obscura's connection to photography to an audience unfamiliar with the device. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Some Renaissance painters used camera obscuras as drawing aids, and the device also works on the same principle as the photographic camera.
In a camera obscura, light passing through a small hole projects an upside-down image onto the opposite wall.
A camera obscura—a dark box or room in which light entering through a small hole projects an image of the outside scene—works on the same basic principle as the photographic camera.
The scholar Ibn al-Haytham described the camera obscura in his Book of Optics in the early eleventh century.
questions.e: The goal has two parts: explain what the device is (for an unfamiliar audience) and link it to photography. Only C does both. A is the strongest trap: it makes the connection but never explains what a camera obscura is. B explains the device without the link to photography, and D gives only history.

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Read every explanation**, including those for questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason, not by luck.

**List your weak skills.** Use your score by skill and write down every skill where you lost two or more questions, plus the trap that caught you (reversed, too extreme, half-right, off-topic, nearest-noun, comma splice…).

**Go back to the matching lessons:** Words in Context and High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences; Sentence Boundaries; Commas and Extra Information; Colons, Dashes and Semicolons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronouns; Verb Tense, Aspect and Finiteness; Modifiers, Parallel Structure and Comparisons; Plurals and Possessives; Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis.
**Redo every question you missed** after the lesson, without looking at the explanation, and say aloud why each wrong choice is wrong.
**Check your timing.** If you did not finish a module, practise with Time Strategy and How to Attack Every Question before your next full test.
